promise: After this you can explain what a publisher, topic and subscription are, how three products fan a message out, and what each promises about delivery and order.

terms.definition: A piece of data one program sends to another.
A server that receives messages and hands them to the programs that want them.
A program that takes messages and does something with them.

before.note: Read Message Queues first: a queue gives each message to one consumer, and pub-sub changes that. The terms here are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: A program often has to tell other programs that something happened, such as an order being placed. If it calls each one directly, it has to know all of them and wait for them. Google's documentation describes the alternative its Pub/Sub service offers: a messaging service between the services that produce messages and the services that process them, so they talk asynchronously instead of through remote procedure calls [[gcp-overview]].

In that description the sender is a publisher and the receiver is a subscriber. Publishers send events to the service without regard to how or when they will be processed, and the service delivers them to all the services that react to them [[gcp-overview]]. The page names topic, publisher and subscriber as its core terms [[gcp-overview]].

The RabbitMQ tutorial draws the line against what you already know from Message Queues. In a work queue, each task is delivered to exactly one worker. In publish/subscribe, a message is delivered to many consumers, and every running copy of the tutorial's receiver program gets the messages [[rabbit-pubsub]]. Google's page adds that its service can also be used as a queue, to spread tasks across workers [[gcp-overview]].

terms.definition: The part of a system that sends a message without choosing who receives it.
A part of a system that has asked to receive messages and gets its own copy of each one.
A named place that publishers send to and subscribers read from.
The sender does not wait for the receiver to finish before carrying on.

stages.name: How it works
body: Each product builds the idea its own way, so the stage describes three of them as theirs. In RabbitMQ, a producer never sends straight to a queue. It sends to an exchange, and a fanout exchange broadcasts every message it receives to all the queues it knows about. A binding is the link that tells an exchange to send to a queue [[rabbit-pubsub]]. In the tutorial's logging example, a message sent when no queue is bound yet is simply discarded, which the tutorial calls fine for that example [[rabbit-pubsub]].

In Kafka, topics are multi-producer and multi-subscriber, and events are not deleted after they are read [[kafka-intro]]. Kafka's design page says a topic is divided into ordered partitions, and each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer within each subscribing consumer group at any given time [[kafka-design]]. So each group sees every message, and consumers inside one group share the work. The diagram draws that.

Google's service uses subscriptions. Its ordering page describes two subscriptions attached to the same topic, both receiving the same set of messages [[gcp-order]]. Google also says its service leases individual messages to subscriber clients and tracks whether each was processed, rather than assigning partitions [[gcp-overview]].

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Two questions decide how much a subscriber can rely on: how many times it may see a message, and in what order. The answers belong to each product. Kafka's design page lists three possible guarantees: at most once, where messages may be lost but are never redelivered; at least once, where they are never lost but may be redelivered; and exactly once, where each is processed once and only once. It also warns that exactly-once claims need reading with care [[kafka-design]]. In Kafka, which one a consumer gets depends on when it saves its position: saving before processing risks losing work after a crash, and processing before saving risks repeating it [[kafka-design]].

Redis says its Pub/Sub is at-most-once: a message is delivered once if at all, and if the subscriber cannot handle it, it is lost for good. For stronger guarantees it points to Redis Streams [[redis-pubsub]]. Google says its service delivers each message at least once, so it might redeliver [[gcp-order]].

Order is likewise per product. Kafka writes events with the same key to the same partition, and a consumer reads a partition in the order it was written [[kafka-intro]]. Google orders messages that share an ordering key, only on subscriptions where ordering is turned on. Messages with different keys are not expected to arrive in order, and a redelivery of one message triggers redelivery of the later ones for that key [[gcp-order]]. Redis says subscribers receive messages in the order they were published [[redis-pubsub]].

A message that keeps failing needs somewhere to go. Google can forward a message it cannot get acknowledged to a dead-letter topic after about a configured number of delivery attempts. The count is approximate, because forwarding is best-effort [[gcp-dlq]].

terms.definition: Kafka's wording: messages may be lost but are never redelivered.
Kafka's wording: messages are never lost but may be redelivered.
Kafka's wording: each message is processed once and only once.
A string, such as a customer ID, that marks messages that should be received in order.
A topic that receives messages a subscriber could not acknowledge.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Every subscriber has its own pace and its own backlog. Kafka keeps events after they are read [[kafka-intro]], while Redis does not keep a message once it has been sent [[redis-pubsub]], so a slow or absent reader loses very different things in the two. Asking what happens when a subscriber is slow, down or crashes halfway through is the first question to put to any system.

Google's overview describes a trade-off it made. Systems that scale with partitions force subscribers to process each partition in order and limit concurrent clients to the number of partitions, while its per-message leasing allows more parallelism [[gcp-overview]]. That is one vendor's view, and Google's ordering page shows what it costs: order is kept only per key and only where it is switched on [[gcp-order]]. The Uber post on the topic page is about the same partition limit in Kafka, and how one company worked around it.

Scope matters too. Google's overview says its service is meant for service-to-service communication, not for end-user or IoT clients, and points to other products for those and for asynchronous service calls [[gcp-overview]]. It is a hosted service, while the Kafka quickstart starts a server on your own machine [[kafka-quickstart]]. The Spotify post on the topic page shows a company that chose a managed pub-sub service and split its events into one topic per type.

misconceptions.myth: Pub-sub always delivers every message to every subscriber, reliably.
misconceptions.truth: It depends on the product. Redis calls its Pub/Sub at-most-once, so a message can be lost [[redis-pubsub]]. Google delivers at least once, so a message can repeat [[gcp-order]]. In Kafka, whether work is lost or repeated depends on when the consumer saves its position [[kafka-design]].

misconceptions.myth: Messages always arrive in the order they were published.
misconceptions.truth: Kafka keeps order inside a partition, and the same key goes to the same partition [[kafka-intro]]. Google keeps order per ordering key, and only when ordering is on for the subscription [[gcp-order]]. Redis says subscribers receive messages in publish order [[redis-pubsub]]. Check what your system promises.

misconceptions.myth: A queue and pub-sub are two different things you must choose between.
misconceptions.truth: Google's overview says its pub-sub service can also be used as a queue to spread tasks across workers [[gcp-overview]]. In Kafka, consumers in one group share a partition's work while each group sees everything [[kafka-design]]. The RabbitMQ tutorial shows both patterns in one broker [[rabbit-pubsub]].

misconceptions.myth: Once a subscriber has read a message, it is gone.
misconceptions.truth: Kafka does not delete events after they are consumed, and they can be read as often as needed [[kafka-intro]]. Redis does not resend a message once it has been sent [[redis-pubsub]].
